en.title: 09 — Limoges, 2002: “Between Signs and Symbols: The Blue Series”
en.curatorial_statement_markdown:
A generous poem by Hafez, our great master of thought, came to me and guided me towards this series of paintings (*The Blue Series*):

*Upon this emerald portico of the heavens they have written in gold*

*That naught shall endure save the goodness of the generous.*

Although none of the words of this poem have been used in any of the works.

Glad tidings have arrived that the days of sorrow shall not endure;

Just as that did not endure, neither shall this endure.

Though I have become humble as dust in the Beloved’s sight,

The rival too shall not remain thus honoured.

Since the chamberlain strikes down all alike with the sword,

None shall abide forever in the inner sanctuary.

What room is there for gratitude or complaint over designs of good and ill,

When upon the tablet of existence no inscription shall endure?

They say this was the song of Jamshid’s banquet:

“Bring forth the cup of wine, for Jam shall not endure.”

Count it a precious boon, O candle, the union with the moth,

For this commerce shall not endure until the dawn.

O wealthy one, win the heart of the dervish who attends thee,

For the treasury of gold and the hoard of silver shall not endure.

*Upon this emerald portico of the heavens they have written in gold*

*That naught shall endure save the goodness of the generous.*

Despair not of the Beloved’s kindness, O Hafez,

For the imprint of cruelty and the mark of tyranny shall not endure.

en.title: 11 — Tarbes, 2004: “Beyond the Body” and Selected Other Works
en.curatorial_statement_markdown:
## Exhibition: “Beyond the Body” and Selected Other Works — Tarbes, France, 2004

My search is focused on finding another gaze upon the cultural evolution of Persia, which has continued from millions of years before humanity to the present day. With Islam, the depiction of the body was forbidden; art and literature came to manifest themselves around architecture, poetry, and calligraphy. Indeed, that three-dimensional bond—architecture, poetry, and calligraphy—conceals within itself three possibilities of human knowledge: the trace of The Real (geography, way of life, climate, nature, plants, flowers, and deserts); the trace of The Imaginary (dreams, desires, hopes, and wishes); and finally the trace of The Symbolic (inscription within culture, in gestures, traits, words, ways of moving, bodily movement, ways of turning the eyes, dances, and so forth), in which repressed elements can emerge, and deep strata of mythology, architectural elements, rituals, and foundational principles reveal themselves. What I seek within this sensibility is an image of the connection and harmony of this form “from a parallel world” through calligraphy and painting: the image of architecture in painting, the image of drawing and curves in calligraphy, the curves of domes within the alphabet—and perhaps, in the future, even deeper traces of symbolisation: the imprints of prehistoric art within these signs and symbols.

My works seek to carry you into an imaginary realm in which ideas and a gaze upon life are inscribed with a mixture of colours—a world in which the magic of time unfolds. My calligraphic lines wish to dance, the harmony of a hand gliding across centuries of history; and within the mysterious labyrinth of Persian poetry, the colours now open the gaze onto an Impressionist world, now rest upon the delicacy of Iranian miniature.

en.title: 12 — Paris, 2005: “The Plates”
en.curatorial_statement_markdown:
## Exhibition: “The Plates” — Paris, 2005

### Hafez and the Dance of Characters on Our Plates

And Hafez comes onto the plate.

Hours of practice and hours of writing calligraphy on paper with the reed pen (*qalam*) prepared me for a journey alongside my ancestors in search of origins: how was a language invented? How were scripts invented? And then Hafez never leaves me; he has been there since I was 14 years old—fragments of his poetry present themselves, remain for as long as they wish, and then suddenly depart.

One day, after hours of practice in the presence of Hafez and my ancestors, I found myself before a plate, and before picking up the knife and fork, I saw in the whiteness of the plate the characters dancing and the calligraphy continuing... What you have before your eyes is the continuation of my research, reaching beyond the medium of paper...

en.title: 07 — Paris, 2001: “Calligraphy, Sign and Symbol”
en.curatorial_statement_markdown:
Exhibition — Paris, 2001

Signs can live individually, separately, without any particular support, without any link between them, across different eras and within varied cultures. Yet signifiers and symbols live amongst one another; they are subjects of exchange: each symbol has a past, it is the product of other symbols and, in turn, generates new ones. Alphabets and the characters of language (musical, mathematical...) form a linked chain that expands the horizon of our world and our culture, of our knowledge and our learning. The white, the void—that non-sign between signs—is a chain as well, a chain extending to infinity, yielding a painting entitled “Nothing”. Meaning reaches us from the space between the signs. In my dreams, and in the works that stand before you, I seek these empty spaces and their meanings...

en.curatorial_statement_markdown:
## Exhibition in Limoges, France, 1999 — “Fusional Love”

More than fifteen years ago, when I placed the titles of the paintings in this series side by side to prepare the exhibition catalogue, they seemed to me to form an expressive poem:

When I look, the clouds are not so far away,[*]
Like love without a reason,
Like the voice of a hand making “the other” dance,
They show the strange paths of the birth of the universe,
Like bodies extending themselves in freedom,
They say to me: look, we are fairer than flowers,
They warm my heart—this voice of the world, this voice of the desert.
Like a hand that sings,
Like my arms holding you tight even when you are not there,
Like clouds so far and so near, turning with the void around them,
Like time turning as they dance,
Like my wings flying in the emptiness of my memories,
Which I seek behind me and find before me—yes, my clouds,
And I run towards them, and the weight of my body leaves me,
Like the planting of my colours upon the carpets that lived with me,
Like mirrors facing one another, the clouds are not so far away.

*This verse is taken from a poem written by a Limousin schoolboy in 1997; it sums up “the story”.

Hassan MAKAREMI, psychoanalyst, painter, and calligrapher, was born in Shiraz, Iran, in 1950.

https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/morceaux-colores-3.jpg

Since 1983, he has lived and worked in France, and has organised some twenty exhibitions of his works in France, the United States, and Russia, including at UNESCO in Paris in 2009.

Drawing on his psychoanalytic knowledge, the Iranian artist Hassan Makaremi has for more than twenty years cast a different gaze upon Persian culture in an approach linking its foundational pillars: poetry, architecture, and calligraphy.

Over fifteen centuries, the Persians introduced two major transformations to their scripts:

- the thickness of the strokes evolved
- the angles became variable

subsequently, an interplay of harmonisation of curves took the place of straight strokes and angles.

Through the invention of a “calligraphy-painting”, Hassan Makaremi’s works allow us to grasp the beauty and delicacy of this script.

https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/morceaux-colores-4.jpg

“What I seek is the illustration of the coherence and harmony of the image of architecture in painting, the image of drawings and curves in calligraphy, the curves of domes in the alphabets...

To surrender to the influence of characters, freeing oneself from time, swimming within these signs, being touched by the rain of words—that is my passion.”

en.curatorial_statement_markdown:
## Exhibition: “Beyond the Body” — Limoges, France, 2003

Beyond the body, invisible traces: through a passage of the lines of the body, lines are there that cannot be seen; I rewrote them in calligraphy, as painting—my surroundings, three birds in one bird.

Seeing, hearing, feeling, ourselves and our exterior, that “Real” which plays with us, which makes us play, which awaits us just a few steps away, beyond our accessible field. And yet, the moment we arrive, this “Real” turns the corner and hides behind: behind a word, a gaze, a sensation, a sound, a stain, a smile. And we remain weary, misunderstood, without bearings, abandoned.

And the endless circle begins anew.

In this series of works before you, forget bodies, lines, colours, supports, names, signifiers and your signifieds! Close your eyes and let the first sensation arrive: “beyond the body”! Trapping the “Real”, that point which shines in the darkness of your closed eyes.

One day, this closed space, without exit, thanks to the immense effort of life will break open, and the true light will dazzle us.

In the meantime, allow me to invite you for a few moments towards this beyond—beyond my “cat”, my “horse”, my “house”, my “parents”, my “musician” friend, one of my “August days”, my “vision of the third second after the Big Bang”, the “fireplace” of my living room, my Statue of Liberty... of my “universe”.

en.title: 18 — Novgorod, 2010: International Exhibition of Calligraphy
en.curatorial_statement_markdown:
## [Novgorod: 3rd International Exhibition of Calligraphy](http://calligraphy-expo.com/eng/Personalities/Participants/Hassan_Makaremi/Biography.aspx?ItemID=59)

Article published in [Plume No. 55, December – January – February 2011](http://www.plume-mag.com/magazine/55/novgorovd-3e-exposition-internationale-de-calligraphie)

(Launched in 1994, *Plume*, the magazine of written heritage, is a quarterly periodical on fine paper richly illustrated in colour, addressed to all enthusiasts and admirers of scripts, manuscripts, and correspondence, as well as to all curious readers interested in history, literature, and the arts.)

News

After Saint Petersburg and Moscow in 2008 and 2009 respectively, it was the turn of Novgorod, a city with a rich historical and artistic past, to host from 10 to 12 September last this fair organised by the Contemporary Museum of Calligraphy in Moscow. “This rare and original art that is calligraphy is highly prized in Russia,” confides Alexey Shaburov, its director, “and that is why we launched such an exhibition.”¹ Supported by local authorities, the event welcomed no fewer than 37,000 visitors, proof of its success. Across an area of 2,000 m², some 200 carefully selected works by more than 35 contemporary calligraphers from across Europe and other continents were displayed on the walls of the sumptuous pavilion erected for the occasion on the banks of the Volkhov. Marked by the diversity of their styles and sources of inspiration, these calligraphic works often belong to pure artistic creation rather than fine penmanship. The expression of a culture, indeed of a civilisation, they convey differing aspirations from one country to another.

Thus, the works of the Russian artist Egor Lobusov turn more towards the quest for ancestral signs, whereas those of the French artists Hassan Makaremi and Michel d’Anastasio belong more to artistic practice. Certain calligraphies, notably those from the Near and Middle East, as well as from the Far East or Eastern Europe, are underpinned by tradition, often religious. The three great religions are indeed sources of inspiration for many of the creations exhibited. Two clearly defined spaces were even dedicated to these “sacred” writings. In one of them, visitors could admire the longest parchment scroll in the world entered in the Guinness Book of Records: a mezuzah² measuring 110 cm in width. Abecedaries, calligrams, and other exercises in visual writing are rather the hallmark of the Latin script, in which French practitioners such as Jean Larcher distinguish themselves, alongside Russian, Scandinavian, English, German, and Italian calligraphers.

Characterised by a great variety of supports—in which one may recognise, besides diverse ranges of paper, parchment, vellum, fabric, porcelain, and birch bark—contemporary calligraphy stands in the wake of a long and ancient practice drawing from the springs of writing and art, continuously associating and blending them in a lyrical breath that is at times breathtaking.

Pascal Fulacher

en.title: 08 — Pompadour, 2002: “Between Sign and Symbol”
en.curatorial_statement_markdown:
### Exhibition: “Between Sign and Symbol” — Pompadour, France, 2002

Painting exhibition of Hassan MAKAREMI

Monday 17 June 2002 to 14 September 2002 — Chapelle de la Jumenterie, Haras National

La Rivière, Arnac-Pompadour, Corrèze

Signs can live individually, separately, without any particular support, without any link between them, across different eras and within varied cultures. Yet signifiers and symbols live amongst one another; they are subjects of exchange: each symbol has a past, it is the product of other symbols and, in turn, generates new ones.

Alphabets and the characters of language (musical, mathematical...) form a linked chain that expands the horizon of our world and our culture, of our knowledge and our learning. The white, the void—that non-sign between signs—is a chain as well, a chain extending to infinity, yielding a painting entitled “Nothing”.

Meaning reaches us from the space between the signs. In the works that stand before you, I seek these empty spaces and their meanings...

I have long believed that Iranian calligraphy—Nastaliq—bears a profound relationship with our surrounding environment and our architecture, the architecture of the desert and even images of the desert, and that our master calligraphers accomplished this by drawing inspiration from nature and flowers, and even through calligraphy combined with Persian poetry.

In Islam, even depicting the human body and painting were virtually forbidden; consequently, all Iranian artistry and delicacy were reflected in tilework, illumination, script, poetry, and even theatrical plays, and our stories too are cast in verse.

I have been researching this question for twenty years, and in this celebration that UNESCO has named the Festival of Cultural Diversity, it has sought for us to celebrate the diversity of cultures. Various activities, such as concerts, are planned.

One of the events on the programme is a lecture by Master Fan Zeng, who is one of the most eminent and greatest Chinese calligraphers and painters. He and I will speak about our perspective on Chinese script and its origins; I will also speak about the origins of script in general, from cuneiform through the families of scripts down to Nastaliq, demonstrating what influence Iranian architecture, and even climate and desert flowers, have had on the Nastaliq script, while half of my time will be devoted to speaking about my own works.

In fact, psychoanalytic research and perspective enabled me, in anthropology, to view Persian script, architecture, and Persian art within the grand context of historical roots stretching back thirty or forty thousand years. What Iranians demonstrated through the Nastaliq script is how to bring together and harmonise architecture, script, poetry, and the entirety of Iranian sensibility with Iranian nature.

In 2005, Dr Changizi, a professor at the Polytechnic University in New York, showed that the origin of all scripts invented in the world lies in small elements that correspond to the curves and lines most frequently observed in nature—meaning that our scribes and calligraphers brought script closer to nature and to Iranian sensibility and life.

I wish to present this as a discovery on which I have been working for twenty years—and which in 2005 was also demonstrated scientifically—because we need both artistic research and scientific research; each complements the other and offers a concrete example in this regard.

Through my own paintings, I show, for instance, how when we look at a dome from the outside, it is constructed upon the same four directions (*chahar-su*); when you look closely at it and unfold its petals, it resembles a desert flower that has opened wide. I have pursued and developed these ideas through painting and drawing.

The National Library of Russia presents the international exhibition project "Incarnated Word. Calligraphy: Text and Image".

The purpose of the project is to showcase the global experience of modern calligraphy, the succession of national schools, and the dialogue between cultures. The artists' works illustrate both the continuity of tradition and innovative artistic solutions. The exhibition brings together the works of established masters of calligraphy alongside the outcomes of the educational process "Master to Student", transmitting the timeless artistic values of the written word. en.title: Prehistoric Art and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights Exhibition, Paris 2005
en.curatorial_statement_markdown:
### Exhibition: Prehistoric Art and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Paris 2005

By voluntarily drawing, with their own hand, the very first line upon a cave wall, humankind took a decisive step: declaring its distinction from the animal world, standing yet more upright, looking further ahead, saying "I can and I know", liberating itself, and advancing its symbolism. This singular relationship with self and world had an anti-death effect upon humanity: life became less mortal, the line endured, carrying its inscribed message across time for future generations.

This human figure playing a wind instrument—with the traces of its music depicted like dots beneath the instrument—that square upon the chief's arm, surviving to this very day as an insignia of rank; sun-worshipping rituals expressing their faith and demonstrating the right to hold belief; family life, a village, and communal life; the right to pleasure, through drawings of the nude body; the right to travel, by recounting its stories; by honouring scenes of production and, finally, of modelling and form-giving—more and more, they express their world through symbols; a right that is as much psychic as it is social...

From bacteria to *Homo sapiens* spans more than 3 billion years, and 40,000 years separate that emergence from our own time. Life continues, and the more the years accumulate, the greater grows the resistance against death of "this thing" which, for simplicity, we call "life"—as though the purpose of living had always been "life" pitted against "death". This vast path towards "pleasure" (*jouissance*), passing through a vital stage that I call the stage of "human rights", cannot come to a halt before reaching the right to life, as the sole foundational right of our shared home, "the Earth". Beyond the fossils of our ancestors and the historical and architectural testimonies that remain as witnesses to this journey, there is prehistoric art, there are writings, there is oral culture, human cultural heritage, and all the living specimens of our Earth. This path still has bright days ahead: indeed, to inscribe the right to life is to establish it.

Perhaps—perhaps this right will guide us beyond this Earth. And perhaps this right will ask of us another space! To continue bequeathing the legacy of "life" to our children, each of us must trace this shared path of living, each according to their own means... "Silence is blue to the height of the sky's eyes; time flows to the measure of our weariness."

The sky beholds us just as we behold it. Yes, it has eyes. Yes, between us and the sun lies this awe-inspiring vastness of silence, with no room for calculation; thus an instrument other than mere accounting is required.

---

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, with its preamble and its thirty articles—the very framework of the structure of our city—stands as the summit of the long march of our forebears' collective life: from the caves towards the moon. From the earliest traces of symbolisation—rock and cave paintings—to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, this span of some forty thousand years of effort and struggle to expand the horizons of our knowledge and well-being is a long crossing.

The eighty thousand fields of prehistoric drawings discovered to date (40,000–8,000 BCE), across the five continents, with the diversity of their symbolisations and the media employed, speak of hope, of travel, of the yearning for peace, of family life, of discovery, of wonder before the cosmos, and finally of relations with the other and with nature... I hear the very same voice when gazing upon prehistoric rock art as when reading the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. What stands before you has no ambition other than to share with you, with our ancestors, and with humankind today this message of continuity: life.

en.title: An Exhibition of Pathways (Parcours)
en.curatorial_statement_markdown:
### An Exhibition of Pathways (Parcours), Paris 2006

Prehistoric art is among the earliest testimonies to humanity's struggle to proclaim its rights. Allow me to begin with a poem by Saadi, one of the most renowned Iranian poets of the thirteenth century CE, for this work reveals how vital Nasta'liq calligraphy on ceramic—inscribed with the humanist verse "Human beings are members of a single body"—is to our gathering today. Through this work, a subtle, invisible thread emerges, deeply binding Nasta'liq calligraphy, architecture, our environment, and, ultimately, Iranian painting and poetry.

Human beings are members of a single body,

Created from one and the same essence.

When time brings pain upon a single limb,

The other limbs cannot remain at rest.

You, who feel no sorrow for the suffering of others,

Deserve not to bear the name of human.

Various studies have been conducted on the origins of humankind, on the roots of the one hundred and forty thousand languages we have created and spoken, and on the path traversed between prehistoric art and writing. These enquiries remind us that "in the beginning", human beings were not nearly as distant from one another as we imagine.

I wish to turn the gaze inward so as to lay bare the fruit of a knowledge and cognition that draws at once upon intuitive and scientific capacity for understanding—for psychoanalysis stands as the turning point between art and knowledge. Opening new horizons, harnessing collaboration between scientific method and the role of intuitive investigation and perception in the service of innovation: this is what profoundly preoccupies me. It is an alchemy negotiating between this interior and exterior, between instinct and cognition, between the artist's freedom and scientific rigour—and equally, where calligraphy is concerned, between the artist's rigour and scientific freedom: the language of nature and the written record of human experience.

It took me twenty years of experience to discover another "place"—a word denoting "time-space"—the lived experience of duality: East–West, The Symbolic–The Real, instinct–experience, another line within a four-dimensional volume. What I wish to share with you, in response to your generosity and your presence here, is this insight: our existence is a passage through a volume, from one point to another, singular and unique; yet this volume of presence inhabits a universal "space-time" of at least thirteen billion human beings—I am not alone.

---

#### Pathways (*Parcours*)

More than three billion years separate bacteria from humankind (*Homo sapiens*), and forty thousand years separate that advent from our own day. Life continues, and the more the years accumulate, the greater grows the resistance against death of "this thing" which, for simplicity, we call "life"—as though the purpose of life were "life" against "death".

This colossal pathway of *jouissance*, passing through a crucial stage of human rights, cannot stop short of reaching the right to life itself, as the sole right of our foundation: "the Earth".

Beyond the fossils of our ancestors and the historical and architectural witnesses that remain as testimonies to this pathway, there is prehistoric art, there are writings, there is oral culture, there are the cultural heritages of humanity, and there is the totality of living spaces upon our Earth—and, evidently, their treasures as a witness to the past as well as a point of departure towards the future.

Until the day when humankind inscribed upon a medium the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and the human being stood forth as the noblest witness to those three billion years.

This Pathway still has bright days ahead: to write the right to life and, of course, to ensure that it is respected.

Perhaps—perhaps this right will lead us beyond this Earth! And perhaps—perhaps this right asks of us another space!

To continue bequeathing this legacy, "life", to our children, it remains for each of us to trace this collective pathway of life, each upon their own medium...

Before you stand the series of works: *From Sign to Symbol* and *From Invisible Lines to Boundless Colour*. It is my pathway across three levels—universal, individual, and artistic—that I share with you.

And I share with you these calligraphies: the harmonious trace of our ancestors' writings along this pathway; these invisible lines, the traces of our dreams in The Real; the silences of the blues.

And it is for you to answer me.

Little time remains to us. If you would also tell me of your pathway... whenever you wish...

"Silence is blue to the height of the sky's eyes,

Time flows to the end of our weariness."

Hassan Makaremi, 2006

en.title: Limoges, France, 1998: Trace of Time in Persian Calligraphy
en.curatorial_statement_markdown:
The Persians replaced their cuneiform script with the Arabic alphabet. This alphabet of fewer than thirty characters was essentially composed of uniform strokes meeting at ninety-degree angles. Over fifteen centuries, the Persians introduced two major transformations: the thickness of the strokes evolved and the angles became variable; subsequently, an interplay of harmonising curves took the place of rigid strokes and angles.

Over centuries, with patience and passion, the masters of Persian calligraphy sought to bring this calligraphy into harmony with the totality of Persian culture. Contemporary Iranian artists, through the invention of a "calligraphy-painting", allow us to sense the beauty and delicacy of this script. The publishing industry, printing presses, and word processors have not aided the advancement of these calligraphic explorations.

To surrender oneself to the influence of the characters, freeing oneself from time; to swim within these signs, to be touched by the rain of words; to allow time to set phrases and verses into play—this is my passion, laid before your eyes.

Where are those characters that flowed from the hands of masters a thousand years ago across manuscript books? Where are those words burned by the Mongols? Where are those poems lost in the deserts, dissolved into the imaginings, dreams, and longings of a people? Where are those curves through which a people beholds the mirror of the universe? I seek them...

en.title: Second Exhibition, Paris 1997: Light, Time, Space
en.curatorial_statement_markdown:
### Exhibition "Light, Time, Space" in Paris, 1997

In brief, in Iranian mythology, "the Earth" is an angel (a *yazata*) in the heavens (the Celestial Earth, *Zamin-e Minavi*); our body dwells upon the physical earth, while our soul (*ravan*) resides in the Celestial Earth. After death, we return to the Celestial Earth. (There appears to be a profound relationship between the Celestial Earth, the Persian garden, and the design of the Persian carpet.) True geography is structured upon seven climes (*haft keshvar*), with Iran at the centre and six realms surrounding it.

> *For your sake Hafez has entered the clime of existence;*
> *Take a step to bid him farewell, for he is about to depart (ravan).*

(Here *ravan* can carry two meanings: the soul—the "celestial I"—and *ravan* in the sense of setting forth.) Ahura Mazda, the Lord of Lords, is Light and our Creator. The sole path to apprehending Being and the self lies in communion with the *ravan* (that part of the "I" which dwells in the Celestial Earth). Only through this path shall we attain complete knowledge, the "Perfect Human" (*Ensan-e Kamel*), and the "Station of the Spiritual Guide" (*Maqam-e Pir*). Striving to reach and commune with the celestial self through Illumination (*Eshraq*) is the very path of Light—or, in other words, "Love". It is not without reason that the Persian word *Mehr* signifies both the sun, generator of light, and love.

https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/wsb_421x531_peinture-300706-015.jpg Poster — Paris: "Lumière, Temps, Espace"

> *You are no less than a mote—do not demean yourself; cultivate love,*
> *So that, whirling in ecstatic dance, you may reach the inner sanctuary of the sun.*

Ahura Mazda and the six other *yazatas* are all deities of Reason and Intellect. ("In the name of the Lord of Soul and Wisdom" — Ferdowsi.) Ahura Mazda is Light and Power. The Angel of the Earth, or Celestial Earth—a feminine deity corresponding to a distant notion of Paradise in the Iranian imagination—is in a sense the emblem of nature's beauty and the emblem of woman's beauty. In a sense, attaining the "other I" inhabiting the "Celestial Earth", which passes through Illumination and Love, is achieved through "unreason" (*bi-kheradi*); the sign of unreason is intoxication, and intoxication is attained through "wine" (*mey*). (For further explanation, see Henry Corbin's introduction to Sheikh Ruzbihan's book *Abhar al-Ashiqin* [*The Jasmine of the Lovers*].)

---

> "To encounter the Earth" not as an aggregate of physical facts, but in the person of its Angel, is an essentially psychic event that can take place neither in the world of impersonal abstract concepts nor on the plane of mere sensory data. The Earth must be perceived not by the senses, but through a primordial image; and because this image bears the features of a personal figure, it proves itself to be symbolising with the soul's very own image of itself, borne in its innermost depth.

> "It is in fact the eighth clime. This suprasensible mystical Orient, place of origin and return, object of the eternal quest, stands at the celestial pole."

> "Orientation in time: the different ways in which humankind confirms its presence upon earth, and the continuity of this presence in something like a history, raising the question of whether it has a meaning... Now, one of the leitmotifs of Iranian Sufi literature is the quest for the Orient... an Orient which, as we understand straightaway, is neither situated nor situatable upon our geographical maps; this Orient is not comprised within any of the seven climes (the *Keshvar*)...

> ... Orientation is a primary phenomenon of our presence in the world. What is proper to a human presence is to spatialise a world around itself, and this phenomenon implies a certain relation of the human being to their world, a relation determined by the very mode of their presence in the world. The four cardinal points—East and West, North and South—are not things encountered by this presence, but directions expressing its meaning, its acclimatisation to its world, its familiarity with it. To possess this sense is to orient oneself in the world. The ideal lines from East to West, from North to South, form a network of *a priori* spatial self-evidences, without which there would be neither geographical nor anthropological orientation..."

> "Whatever name one gives it, the events that determine the relationship with the invisible personal guide do not fall within quantitative physical time; they are not measurable by the chronological units of time—homogeneous and uniform, governed by the motions of the stars; they do not insert themselves into the continuous web of irreversible events. These events unfold in a time indeed, yet a time uniquely their own: that discontinuous, purely qualitative psychic time whose moments can be evaluated only according to their own measure—a measure varying each time with their very intensity. And this intensity measures a time in which the past remains present to the future, and in which the future is already present to the past, just as the notes of a musical phrase, sounded successively, nonetheless all persist together in the present precisely to constitute that phrase."

— H. CORBIN

"Henry Corbin": seconded in 1935 by the Bibliothèque nationale to the Institut Français de Berlin, he brought back from there the first French translation of Heidegger's *"What Is Metaphysics?"* Charged with missions in Turkey and subsequently in Iran, he founded the Department of Iranology at the Franco-Iranian Institute. He is the author of a vast fresco of the principal stages of Islamic thought from its origins to the great philosophers of seventeenth-century Iran under the title *History of Islamic Philosophy in Iranian Islam* (*En Islam iranien*), four volumes devoted to Iranian, Shiite, Ismaili, and Sufi thinkers that revealed to the West an unknown spiritual continent. He died in Paris in 1978.

en.title: The Conference of the Birds Painting — Paris, 2008
en.curatorial_statement_markdown:
## Exhibition: The Painting "The Conference of the Birds" (*Mantiq al-Tayr*), Paris 2008

This painting, measuring 210 by 1,000 centimetres, was created in Paris in 2006 and 2007 on the basis of the epic poem *The Conference of the Birds* (*Mantiq al-Tayr*) by the revered Farid al-Din Attar of Nishapur. Beginning from the right with the verse *"The birds of the world held an assembly"*, it opens with the image of the globe and the birds gathered around it, and points towards the seven stages and valleys through which these birds were destined to pass. At the end, with the rising of the sun, thirty birds (*si morgh*) arrive at Mount Qaf, where the shadow of that cloud is none other than the Simorgh itself. At this stage, on the right side, stands a convex mirror in which all the birds—just as Attar tells us—behold themselves and all that has come to pass, and the viewer does likewise.

[A short film introducing this painting](/en/media/videos/simorq-tablo-ir)

The experience of the mystical journey, an exemplar of observing life through the mystical school of the tenth to fourteenth centuries CE — the Seven Valleys:

- **First Valley — The Valley of Quest (*Talab*):** Awakening; a living being enters life, takes hold of its destiny, and advances amidst critical and arduous conditions—from Christopher Columbus to Yuri Gagarin—towards the sky, upon the moon, or within thought and imagination, in search of the essence of life which, like the alchemists, one may call *"latifah"* (the subtle essence).

- **Second Valley — The Valley of Love (*Eshq*):** The driving force and motive energy, across diverse definitions of love: Sigmund Freud considers its foundational model to be the mother–child relationship—a state of unity woven from separation and attachment, a state that enables us to perceive the "Other", an Other who may be indefinable, overwhelmingly close, something that after awakening forbids us from falling back asleep; birth and renewal.

- **Third Valley — The Valley of Knowledge (*Ma'refat*):** Knowledge of one's own presence after birth; this presence allows each of us to recognise the Other through observation, comparison, and the emergence of the symbol—from prehistoric art to our place today...

- **Fourth Valley — The Valley of Independence (*Esteghna*):** If I am one element among other elements, I hold an equal value and can receive nothing beyond my rightful measure. Let us listen to Hafez, celebrant of love, a bird from another world:

> *Such a cage ill befits a sweet-voiced singer like me;*
> *I shall fly to the Garden of Paradise, for I am a bird of that meadow.*

- **Fifth Valley — The Valley of Unity (*Yeganegi*):** After such knowledge and such union comes the first sense of arrival, companionship, and discernment. In this domain within Iranian mysticism, *Hu* signifies "He", or more simply the "Other"—only the "Other" exists.

- **Sixth Valley — The Valley of Astonishment (*Heyrat*):** Astonishment before the abyssal depth of my place; my eyes open wide and I see afar—in an eternal, irrevocable manner.

- **Seventh Valley — Poverty and Annihilation (*Faqr va Fana*):** Life, in its utmost simplicity, just as Hafez reveals it:

> *I, dust-stained with spiritual poverty, shame upon my high resolve*
> *If ever I wet the hem of my robe in the waters of the sun's own spring.*

---

### Paris 2008 Exhibition & Literary Launch

Mina and Hassan Makaremi cordially invite you to honour with your presence the **Retrospective** and **Launch of the Poetry Collection *Piano à quatre mains* (*Piano for Four Hands*)**, from 21 to 23 November 2008 at **Galerie de la Cave**, 62 rue du Cardinal-Lemoine, 75005 Paris (Métro: Cardinal Lemoine).

- Friday, 21 November: 4:00 pm to 9:00 pm
- Saturday, 22 November: 4:00 pm to 10:00 pm
- Sunday, 23 November: 3:00 pm to 8:00 pm

*Proceeds from the sales of this exhibition will be donated to the association "Parrainage France-Togo".*

The painting *The Conference of the Birds* (2 metres by 10 metres), the centrepiece of the exhibition, pairs an introduction to the tradition of *Pardeh Dari* with its living practice. In a contemporary idiom, the painting recounts the essence of the tale of *The Conference of the Birds*, grounded in the myth of the Simorgh. In Persian mythology, the figure of the Simorgh dwelling upon the mythical Mount Qaf holds supreme significance.

This 20-square-metre canvas was created between 2005 and 2007. In it, I illustrate the narrative of *The Conference of the Birds* (*Mantiq al-Tayr*) by Farid al-Din Attar, the Persian poet who lived from 1119 to 1190 and belongs to the great Iranian mystical tradition (*Le Langage des oiseaux*, Pocket edition, Farid al-Din Attar, translated by Garcin de Tassy).

*The Conference of the Birds* comprises 4,647 verses. It is a mystical epic in which the birds set forth in search of their King. The narrative opens with a welcoming discourse fulfilling a ritual and magical function that brings together the "Hoopoe", a crowned bird, and the other birds, who represent a seeking humanity. Forthwith, the throng of anxious birds assembles, and providentially the Hoopoe presents itself as messenger. It exhorts the birds to embark upon a demanding journey that will lead them to the court of their King, a fabulous bird: the Simorgh.

All the birds grasp the fundamental significance of this undertaking; yet almost immediately the majority offer excuses. The Hoopoe admonishes them all, calms some, encourages others, and begins the instruction that will enable them to set out upon the journey. They must enter the seven valleys marking the initiatory degrees of their spiritual ascent.

These mystical valleys are the valleys of Quest, Love, Knowledge, Independence, Union, Astonishment, and Destitution. Only after traversing these valleys—in a long voyage during which the vast majority of the birds perish—do the survivors find themselves denied, as a final ordeal, the long-hoped-for entry into the palace of their King, the Simorgh. The artistic form chosen is a modern manifestation of *Pardeh Dari*, a pre-Islamic Iranian art form that has undergone two transformations since its origin. ### Exhibition: I Am Not Me — Fez, Morocco, June 2012

### Festival of Sacred Music, Batha Museum

#### "I am not me, not me am I": this is the opening hemistich of a sublime ghazal by Asiri Lahiji, which may recall the discourse of the torus in the Lacanian topology of our psyche. In these three words, the poet puts forward the most fundamental human question: the boundaries of the "I" and the other, or my presence in the being of the other. Such an indivisible and unbreakable "I", through the extraordinary presence of symbolisation and by attaining the dimension of communication made possible through these very symbols, enters into relation with the other and with past, present, and future; the "I" emerges from its state of stasis and creates another "I". Human presence in its world, with the knowledge acquired thus far, can be recalled across four worlds: the tangible and observable world, the measurable world, the possible world, and the world that holds the Subject in its possession. Working upon this profound poem and its relationship with the Lacanian torus and the imaginal world has guided me to the paintings below.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-uoc4SSoBlA

If Our Universe Were a Torus

---

«Man nah manam, nah man manam»
«I am not me, not me, I am»

Asiri, 17th-century Iranian poet

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w-oLvLeKtEU&feature=youtu.be

Between intoxication without the faculty of thought and being awake without being truly enchanted, there is a third place—a time-space that Khayyâm seeks.

#### If Our Universe Were a Torus

"I am not me, not me, I am": this verse declares a state of human being profoundly questioning its boundaries—a presence of the self in an other Universe. This individual, indivisible, who through the magic of symbolisation, through the integration of the dimensions of communication made possible by symbols, and through the fluidity of the circulation of symbols between oneself and the other, between past, present, and future, shatters the immobile status of the individual and invents another self: a self swimming in symbols, with no tie to time or space.

The presence of a human Subject in their Universe concentrates within them their entire culture. From there, the Subject presents their discourse. "I am not me…": this poetic utterance is an introductory step into the negation of the Subject and therefore merits in-depth research. The Universe is individual, even if our knowledge and learning to date direct us towards the classification of at least four families of the Universe: the visible Universe, the measurable Universe, the possible Universe, and the Universe encompassing the presence of a Subject.

The earliest primates allow us to imagine the Universe of the speaking being thanks to traces of gestural symbolisation. Then come intermediary objects, rituals, syllables, words, spoken utterances, prehistoric drawings, and the first elements of writing. The tales of shamans, mythologies, and oral culture present us with another side of this Universe. Dream, fantasy, poetry, and art are other dimensions of it.

Henry Corbin, the great twentieth-century French scholar, by dissecting pre-Islamic Persian culture and mythology and their continuity within the thought of Iranian mystics, reveals to us the presence of a parallel world, which is neither this world nor the other world after death: a clime, a continent present yet inaccessible to us, except for rare exceptions. A part of our presence as a human Subject dwells in this world. It is "Ravan", a concept untranslatable through our notion of psyche—as if this world, the third one, were neither this present, internal world, nor our absent, external world of our imaginable Universe, but squarely between the two.

Jacques Lacan, French psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, speaks of a Universe of signifiers conveyed among "speaking beings" that belongs to no one. Neither internal nor external, in a third place. As if our Universe were a Torus! There is an exterior within the interior, or an interior outside.

A torus is generated by the rotation of one circle around another circle.

What if, ultimately, this exterior-interior or interior-exterior split our Universe differently? Calling the boundaries of the ego into question is perhaps not foreign to this feeling of presence. Beyond symbolisation, there are also traces of self-construction—boundaries difficult to harness with the tools of symbolisation.

If writing is the summit of our ancestors' collective symbolisation enabling entry into the world of science, and if art, music, dance, and the visual arts are noble means of manifesting knowledge and our intuitions, can one say that calligraphy is the stylisation of this symbolisation using the harmony created by art?

What you have before you is an endeavour to bring a history back to life. The Torus Universe, represented by the environmental elements of the Persian world and Nastaliq or Parsi calligraphy and their close relations, embodies the harmony of this atmosphere.

Hassan Makaremi, Paris, 2012

While thinkers and masters of song each give, in their own way, their vision of the "re-enchantment of the world", painters from here and abroad have brought out their brushes to add their touch as well to the canvas of the 18th edition of the Fez Festival of World Sacred Music.

Around the rear garden of the sumptuous Batha Museum, the French painter of Iranian origin Hassan Makaremi, who has titled his exhibition "I Am Not Me, Not Me, I Am", sets out to propose a third "time-space" place, situating it between "intoxication without the faculty of thought and wakefulness without being truly enchanted".

Hassan Makaremi's exhibition shares the walls of the Batha Museum with a faithful daughter of the city, Laila Iraki, who has recently devoted herself to her passion for painting after many years practising as a lecturer at the Faculty of Medicine in Casablanca.

The works in her exhibition, which pays "Homage to My City", reflect all themes relating to nature, without forgetting her keen interest in historical monuments. Gifted in drawing since earliest childhood, she makes no secret of the contribution of the painter Afif Bennani, who generously transmitted to her mastery of the brush and the palette knife.

A few alleyways further on, the Scottish painter Caroline Fulton chose the walls of the handsome Riad Réda to house her exhibition "Our Living Neighbours: Animals of Morocco", which invites the public on a journey into the world of Morocco's animals through her various canvases of diverse styles and colours.

Within a context of abstract and figurative motifs, Caroline Fulton, who resides in Essaouira, conveys through a tender and nostalgic gaze the uncertain condition of these nonetheless familiar animals within the aesthetics of a human environment.

At Dar Tazi, another architectural jewel of the medina, David Packer's exhibition "Astrolabes" challenges preconceived ideas of the world through a visual inspection integrating two particular interests: industry and the natural world. His works represent what at first sight appear to be things of everyday life, familiar objects such as plastic water bottles, car engines, trains, and animals.

These common subjects, sometimes reconfigured with new media and sometimes constructed from found objects, are transformed into objects that resonate with more complex associations. ### Exhibition and Lecture at UNESCO Headquarters in Paris, 19 May 2009

Conversation with Hassan Makaremi, Psychoanalyst, Painter, Calligrapher, and Human-Rights Activist

#### "With the First Line Drawn Deep Inside a Cave, Human Rights Began"

Iraj Adibzadeh

"Let Us Celebrate the Variety and Diversity of Cultures" was the title of the festival organised in Paris in May 2009 by UNESCO, the House of World Cultures affiliated with the United Nations, which came to a close on Sunday, 31 May.

In this special festival, UNESCO opened its doors so that this time—without the interference of various governments, which generally influence each country's special programmes and artists and act as a sort of gatekeeper—it could invite researchers, scholars, and artists to showcase the differences between cultures as well as their interconnections and affinities through exhibitions of painting, calligraphy, books of poetry, conferences, and, of course, musical concerts.

A striking feature of the Festival of Cultural Diversity was the demonstration of the closeness and kinship between the two ancient cultures of China and Iran—specifically through the arts of painting, calligraphy, poetry, and books of verse that have flowed through both cultures for thousands of years. At the conference held during this celebration of cultural diversity at UNESCO, it was shown how these two cultures ultimately converge.

Master Fan Zeng, the Chinese painter, calligrapher, and poet, and Hassan Makaremi, the Iranian psychoanalyst, painter, calligrapher, and human-rights activist, spoke about perspectives on Chinese script and its roots, the origins of script dating back seven thousand years to the present, its influence on architecture, poetry, painting, and miniature art, and the kinship between the two cultures.

At the venue of this conference at UNESCO in Paris, I met with Mr Hassan Makaremi—clinical psychoanalyst, painter, calligrapher, and researcher into the history of script in human life—and asked him about his participation in this conference alongside the Chinese master Fan Zeng, and what message they carry at this gathering.

My profession is psychoanalysis, and it is precisely psychoanalysis that has taken the artistic dimension of my work to another place. In the field of art, for roughly twenty years I have been pursuing the question of origins and the understanding of script in relation to our environment.

I believed that Iranian calligraphy—Nastaliq—bears a profound relationship to our surrounding environment, our architecture, desert architecture, and even desert landscapes, and that our master calligraphers achieved this by drawing inspiration from nature and flowers, and even by combining calligraphy with Persian poetry.

Hassan Makaremi / Photographs: Iraj Adibzadeh

In Islam, even depicting the human body and figurative painting were almost forbidden; consequently, the entirety of Iranian artistry and subtlety found expression in tilework, illumination (*tazhib*), calligraphy, poetry, and even dramatic performances, while our stories too took poetic form.

I have been researching this question for twenty years, and in this celebration that UNESCO has named the Celebration of Cultural Diversity, it has sought to celebrate the diversity of cultures. Various activities, such as concerts, are included in the programme.

One of the items on the programme is the lecture by Master Fan Zeng, who is one of the most eminent and greatest Chinese calligraphers and painters. He and I speak on perspectives regarding Chinese script and its roots, while I also speak on the roots of script generally—from cuneiform to the families of scripts, leading up to Nastaliq—and demonstrate the effects that Iranian architecture, and even climate and desert wildflowers, have had on Nastaliq calligraphy; half of my time is also devoted to speaking about my own works.

In fact, psychoanalytic research and perspective enabled me to examine anthropology, Persian script, and Persian architecture and art within the vast context of thirty- to forty-thousand-year-old historical roots. What Iranians demonstrated through Nastaliq script is how to bring architecture, calligraphy, poetry, and the entirety of Persian sensibility into harmony with Iranian nature.

Mr Changizi, one of the professors at Polytechnic in New York, demonstrated in 2005 that the roots of all scripts invented in the world lie in small component shapes—and these small components are the very curves and lines we observe most frequently in nature. That is to say, our scribes and calligraphers brought script closer to nature and to Iranian sensibility and life.

I wish to present this as a discovery on which I have been working for twenty years—and which was also demonstrated scientifically in 2005—for we need both artistic research and scientific research; each complements the other and offers a concrete example in this regard.

Through my own paintings, I show, for example, how when we look at a dome from the outside, it is constructed upon that same four-quartered symmetry (*chahar-su*). When you look closely at it and unfold its petals, it resembles a desert flower whose petals have opened and scattered. I developed these ideas through painting and drawing.

Hassan Makaremi beside Fan Zeng

At the conference venue, the gaze of the two civilisations of Chinese and Iranian culture was exhibited under the title *The Painting of Human Rights*.

This painting is the natural continuation of my research, expressing a commitment to the human message of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It is the first document written by humanity itself—comprising a preamble and thirty articles—in which everyone believes, and in which the grammar and syntax of human life are laid down; I believe in it deeply.

I strove, using Nastaliq script, thirty poems by Hafez, and years of work on prehistoric painting fields, to arrive at these results. As you know, we have around eighty thousand prehistoric painting sites across the five continents of the world, created between roughly thirty-five thousand and one hundred thousand years ago.

I studied these sites and was able to draw upon them to paint one canvas for each of the articles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. All of these are brought together, and the painting is like the depths of a cave in which they are condensed. For instance, it is shown that twelve thousand years ago, when our forebears depicted a man playing a wind instrument, they placed several dots beneath it—meaning they showed him playing musical notes.

I too wished in a sense to show that the human being who drew the very first line with their own hand deep inside a cave declared: "I am human; I differ from the animal. I am free, and I can draw something whose trace endures for future generations." Not only do I speak, I also draw—and later, I write.

Here is where human rights begin. Human rights are a human-psychological concept, whereas rights in the social sense came into existence afterwards—that is, human rights precede social rights. When in 1792 we write the Declaration of Human Rights in Paris, it is in fact a summary of what humanity has lived, not something invented.

From the works of Hassan Makaremi

Yet how can one support and expand human rights through art?

I think that first and foremost, it is the message itself—just like this painting and the showing of script. The root of all scripts is one, just as it is said: "Human beings are members of one whole / In creation of one essence and soul." When I demonstrate that all scripts and virtually all languages share a single root, a firm foundation for primary human rights is laid at that very juncture.

That is from a general perspective. In everyday terms and personally, whatever is earned from the sale of artwork is spent on human rights. Thirdly, artists can interconnect the human rights system.

For example, Master Fan Zeng, with whom I spoke, is Chinese after all. When he defends nature here, we sit down and converse together. It is the connections among artists with one another that can gradually move towards civil society.

Everyone knows that the path of human rights passes through civil society—that is, that we should be able to create elements through which human beings can come together outside governments. And it seems to me that if UNESCO and any international organisation gives each of us this opportunity to speak our mind as an individual, as an artist, as a scholar, as a researcher, it is our duty to press for international organisations to set governments aside as well.

At UNESCO too, I shall say that UNESCO is the home of the culture of peoples, not the culture of governments. Governments have no culture; their sole function is to preserve the existing position and status quo. For the past two or three years, UNESCO has begun this valuable work of turning towards civil society—

that is, reaching out to individuals who are independent and defenders of human rights, so that if they have something to say, they may come and say it. I have spoken of this very matter with them at length, I encourage it, and I hope it will continue.

Mina Rad beside Indrasen, Secretary-General and organiser of the festival

Next, I asked Mina Rad, journalist and one of the public-relations officers of the Festival of Cultural Diversity at UNESCO, about the aims of the festival and its conference.

This conference allows us to see that even though cultures differ from one another, they are close to one another—and they demonstrated this in a remarkably subtle way through calligraphy and painting. Through calligraphy it becomes clear how Chinese culture and Iranian culture, which have come down to us from thousands of years ago, have each played a role in human evolution across architecture, painting, and poetry.

Mr Fan Zeng and Mr Hassan Makaremi are both painters, calligraphers, poets, and thinkers, and both converge on one path—namely this festival that has connected them—and the discourse they present at this conference shows how the tomorrow of humanity and the tomorrow of diverse cultures and civilisations are linked through one culture looking at another, demonstrating how cultures can relate to one another through showcasing the arts of poetry, culture, and calligraphy.

In conclusion, I speak with Mr Indrasen, Secretary-General and organiser of the Festival of Cultural Diversity at UNESCO, who invited them to the festival's parallel conference, "Two Cultures Looking at One Another".

First of all, this festival is a festival of different cultures looking at one another, and I wished to invite these two cultures to look at each other as in a mirror and reveal the historical and cultural differences and similarities between these two cultures.

Will this method of inviting artists, intellectuals, and independent individuals to UNESCO without government interference continue within this organisation?

Yes; the Festival of Different Cultures complements UNESCO's other cultural activities within the framework we drafted on the theme of the diversity of peoples' cultures. The ultimate objective is to connect different cultures with one another, and this work will continue.

Master Fan Zeng (China)
Born into a distinguished family of Chinese literati, Fan Zeng is one of the best-known Chinese painters in China and Asia. A complete artist, he also excels in calligraphic art and classical poetry.
In China, from the tenth century onwards, "literati painting" became the dominant current in Chinese painting. Thus, a great Chinese painter must excel in the three arts: poetry, calligraphy, and painting. One cannot favour a single one at the expense of the others.
"If a painter does not cultivate the poetic art and calligraphy, he will not be considered a master. A painting without poetry will be a work devoid of spirituality and soul. And a painter whose calligraphy is weak will likewise produce a painting without brilliance," as Fan Zeng puts it, considering himself first a poet and then a calligrapher in order to realise his dream of becoming a great painter.

Hassan Makaremi (Iran)

Drawing on his psychoanalytic knowledge, the Iranian artist Hassan Makaremi has for more than twenty years brought another gaze to Persian culture through an approach linking its fundamental pillars: poetry, architecture, and calligraphy.
Over fifteen centuries, the Persians introduced two major modifications to their scripts:
the thickness of strokes evolved and angles became variable; subsequently, a play of harmonisation of curves took the place of strokes and angles.
Through the invention of a "calligraphy-painting", Hassan Makaremi's works allow us to grasp the beauty and delicacy of this script.
"What I seek is the illustration of the coherence and harmony of the image of architecture in painting, the image of drawings and curves in calligraphy, the curves of domes in alphabets... Letting oneself yield to the influence of characters, freeing oneself from time, swimming in these signs, being touched by the rain of words—that is my passion."

Find Hassan Makaremi on the internal blog of Les Haras nationaux, where you will learn more about the passion that calligraphy represents for him.

Performance at UNESCO

Hassan Makaremi presents his passion for calligraphy:

"For centuries, with patience and passion, the masters of Persian calligraphy sought to bring this calligraphy into harmony with the totality of Persian culture. Letting oneself yield to the influence of characters, freeing oneself from time; swimming in these signs, being touched by the rain of words; letting time bring sentences and verses into play—that is my passion, laid bare before your eyes. Where are those flowing characters from the hands of the masters of a thousand years ago in manuscript books? Where are those words burned by the Mongols? Where are those poems lost in the deserts, melted into the imaginary and the nostalgias of a people? Where are those curves: thanks to them, a people sees the mirror of the universe. I am searching for them…" …
"More than three billion years, from the bacterium to humankind—'Homo sapiens'—and forty thousand years from that advent down to our own days. Life goes on, and the more the years accumulate, the greater grows the resistance against death of 'this thing' which, for simplicity, we call 'life'. As though the purpose of life were 'life' against 'death'.
This colossal trajectory of 'Jouissance', passing through a crucial stage of human rights, cannot stop without advancing all the way to the right of life, as the sole right of our foundation, 'the Earth'.
Beyond the fossils of our ancestors and the historical and architectural witnesses that remain to us as testimonies to this journey: there is rock art, there are writings, there is oral culture, there are human cultural heritages, and there is the totality of living spaces upon our Earth. And evidently there is their capital as a witness to the past as well as the point of departure towards the future.
Until the day when something was written upon a medium: the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and the human being stands forth as the noblest witness to these three billion years.
This trajectory still has bright days ahead of it: writing the right of life, and of course ensuring it is respected.
Perhaps—perhaps this right leads us beyond this Earth! And perhaps—perhaps this right asks of us another space!
To continue leaving this heritage—'life'—to our children, it remains for each of us to trace this collective trajectory of life, yet each upon our own medium…"
